slides.title: The Experience Promise
slides.task_brief:
KEY MESSAGE SLIDE — The Experience Promise.

Title: 'The DeepMindQ Experience Promise' in h2 weight 700, left-aligned.
Blue accent line below.

Central promise statement in large display text (centered, ~1.75rem, weight 600, white):

'Every morning, a VP Sales opens DeepMindQ and within 3 minutes knows exactly what changed, why it matters, who to engage, what to say, and what to do — with full confidence in the evidence behind every recommendation.'

Below the promise, 3 supporting pillars in glass-card grid-3 layout:

Card 1 (blue-tinted border): Icon 'psychology' · Title 'Intelligence, Not Data' · Body: 'We do not show information. We deliver intelligence. Every element answers: what, why, who, how, and why trust this?'

Card 2 (purple-tinted border): Icon 'visibility' · Title 'Confidence at Every Layer' · Body: 'Every recommendation carries an evidence footprint. Users never have to guess why the system suggests something.'

Card 3 (green-tinted border): Icon 'speed' · Title '3-Morning-Minute Protocol' · Body: 'The entire Intelligence Hub experience is designed to deliver complete situational awareness in under 3 minutes.'

Speaker notes: The Experience Promise is our contract with the user. It is not a feature list. It is the outcome we guarantee. Every design decision in MS6 is measured against this promise. If a component, interaction, or flow does not serve this promise, it does not belong in the product.

slides.title: Intelligence as Executive Briefing — Core Principle
slides.task_brief:
KEY MESSAGE SLIDE — Core Principle: Intelligence as Executive Briefing.

Title: 'Core Design Pattern #1' in h2 weight 700, left-aligned.
Subtitle: 'AI Intelligence as Executive Briefing — Not a Command' in primary-dim small text.
Blue accent line below.

Central principle statement (large, centered, ~1.5rem, weight 600, white):

'DeepMindQ does not tell the user what to do.
DeepMindQ briefs the user on what is happening, why it matters, and recommends what to consider — with full evidence transparency.'

Below: 4 distinction cards in grid-2 layout:

Card 1 (blue border): Title 'Briefing, Not Direction' · Body: 'The system presents intelligence as an executive briefing document — structured, prioritized, evidence-backed. The decision always belongs to the human.'

Card 2 (purple border): Title 'Recommendation, Not Instruction' · Body: 'AI suggests actions with confidence levels and evidence trails. Users evaluate, adjust, and decide. The system provides the briefing; the user provides the judgment.'

Card 3 (green border): Title 'Evidence, Not Authority' · Body: 'Every insight carries its evidence footprint. Trust is built through transparency, not through brand or authority. Users can always answer: why does the system think this?'

Card 4 (amber border): Title 'Context, Not Complexity' · Body: 'Progressive disclosure reveals depth on demand. The morning briefing gives the summary; deeper layers are available for those who need them. Intelligence surfaces first; complexity reveals itself when needed.'

Speaker notes: This is Design Pattern #1 and it overrides everything else. The distinction between briefing and direction is subtle but critical. An executive briefing gives the reader context, analysis, and recommendations — but the executive makes the decision. This is the relationship DeepMindQ must have with its users.

slides.title: The 5-Question Framework
slides.task_brief:
BENTO GRID SLIDE — The 5-Question Framework.

Title: 'The 5-Question Morning Intelligence Protocol' in h2 weight 700, left-aligned.
Subtitle: 'Every element of the Intelligence Hub maps to these five questions' in primary-dim.
Blue accent line below.

Bento grid layout (3 columns, varying card heights):

Card 1 (top-left, spans 2 cols, blue border glow): Icon 'notification_important' · Title '1. What Changed?' · Body: 'Surface critical signals — account movements, market shifts, competitive changes, opportunity updates. Ranked by impact, not recency.'

Card 2 (top-right, amber border): Icon 'lightbulb' · Title '2. Why It Matters' · Body: 'Context and reasoning behind every signal. Impact analysis, trend correlation, revenue implication.'

Card 3 (mid-left, purple border): Icon 'people' · Title '3. Who to Engage' · Body: 'Account-specific recommendations. Priority-ranked engagement targets with reasoning.'

Card 4 (mid-center, green border): Icon 'chat' · Title '4. What to Say' · Body: 'Conversation angles, talking points, and contextual intelligence for each engagement.'

Card 5 (mid-right, cyan border): Icon 'rocket_launch' · Title '5. What to Do' · Body: 'Recommended actions with confidence scores, timelines, and evidence trails.'

Card 6 (bottom, spans full width, glass-card accent): Title 'Design Rule' · Body: 'No intelligence element exists in the Hub that does not map to at least one of these five questions. If a component cannot answer which question it serves, it belongs in a deeper experience layer, not the Hub.'

Speaker notes: The 5-Question Framework is the structural backbone of the Intelligence Hub. It is not a feature — it is an information architecture constraint. Every card, signal, recommendation, and action in the Hub must map to one of these five questions. This prevents the Hub from becoming an overloaded dashboard.

slides.title: Progressive Disclosure Model
slides.task_brief:
KEY MESSAGE SLIDE — Progressive Disclosure Model.

Title: 'Design Pattern #2 & #3 — Progressive Disclosure & Cognitive Load Reduction' in h2 weight 700, left-aligned.
Blue accent line below.

4-level progressive disclosure visualization as horizontal stepped cards:

Level 1 — 'DECISION LAYER' (large blue card):
Label: 'What & Why' · Body: 'Headline, confidence score, priority badge, timestamp. The user sees intelligence at a glance — enough to decide: do I need to act on this now?'

Arrow →

Level 2 — 'REASONING LAYER' (medium purple card):
Label: 'Why Does the System Think This?' · Body: 'Primary reasoning statement, positive and negative confidence factors, impact analysis. Answers the trust question before the user asks it.'

Arrow →

Level 3 — 'EVIDENCE LAYER' (smaller green card):
Label: 'Show Me the Proof' · Body: 'Evidence chain with sources, dates, relevance scores, and verification links. Full transparency for users who need to validate.'

Arrow →

Level 4 — 'EXPLORATION LAYER' (smallest amber card):
Label: 'What Else Should I Know?' · Body: 'Related signals, connected insights, adjacent opportunities, and deeper research paths.'

Below the 4 levels, a key principle box (glass-card accent):
'Each level is independently accessible. Users who trust the system stay at L1. Skeptics drill to L3. Researchers explore L4. The experience adapts to the user's trust level — the user is never forced to digest complexity they do not need.'

Speaker notes: Progressive disclosure is the mechanism that makes Intelligence as Executive Briefing work. Not every user needs the same depth. A VP Sales who trusts the system after weeks of use may never drill past Level 1. A new user or a skeptic will want Level 3 evidence. The key insight: each level is independently accessible and answers a specific cognitive need.

slides.title: Trust & Evidence Visualization
slides.task_brief:
BENTO GRID SLIDE — Trust & Evidence Visualization.

Title: 'Design Patterns #6 & #7 — Trust Visualization & Confidence Language' in h2 weight 700, left-aligned.
Blue accent line below.

Bento grid layout with 6 component evaluation cards:

Card 1 (top-left, blue border): Title 'ConfidenceIndicator' · Status badge 'EVALUATE → INCORPORATE' (green) · Body: 'Existing: 4 modes (ring/bar/badge/score), animated, design-tokenized. Assessment: Strong alignment with MS6 principles. Action: Incorporate into Design System as universal confidence display.'

Card 2 (top-right, purple border): Title 'EvidenceChain' · Status badge 'EVALUATE → INCORPORATE' (green) · Body: 'Existing: Visual evidence trail with numbered steps, source icons, relevance scores. Assessment: Core trust pattern. Action: Redesign visual styling to match premium enterprise language while preserving interaction model.'

Card 3 (mid-left, green border): Title 'InlineReasoning' · Status badge 'EVALUATE → INCORPORATE' (green) · Body: 'Existing: Reasoning text + positive/negative factor tags. Assessment: Key L2 surface. Action: Refine factor visualization, add expand-to-evidence link pattern.'

Card 4 (mid-center, amber border): Title 'IntelligenceNarrative' · Status badge 'EVALUATE → REDESIGN' (amber) · Body: 'Existing: 811-line core narrative component, 6 variants, L1-L4 disclosure. Assessment: Right pattern, wrong complexity. Action: Decompose into composable atoms, reduce API surface.'

Card 5 (mid-right, cyan border): Title 'ProgressiveDisclosure' · Status badge 'EVALUATE → REDESIGN' (amber) · Body: 'Existing: 4-level standalone disclosure. Assessment: Concept aligns, but uses inline Tailwind colors instead of design tokens. Action: Unify with token system, merge with IntelligenceNarrative pattern.'

Card 6 (bottom-right, red border): Title 'RecommendationCard' · Status badge 'EVALUATE → REDESIGN' (amber) · Body: 'Existing: 524-line account recommendation display, fetches its own data. Assessment: Too monolithic, violates separation of concerns. Action: Split into data layer and presentation layer.'

Speaker notes: We evaluated all 6 existing Intelligence OS components against MS6 principles. Three components — ConfidenceIndicator, EvidenceChain, and InlineReasoning — align well and will be incorporated with refinements. Three components — IntelligenceNarrative, ProgressiveDisclosure, and RecommendationCard — have the right conceptual patterns but need significant redesign to meet cognitive load reduction and premium enterprise standards. The key takeaway: we are not throwing away existing work. We are unifying it into one consistent experience language.

slides.title: Emotional Design DNA
slides.task_brief:
KEY MESSAGE SLIDE — Emotional Design DNA.

Title: 'Design Patterns #8–#11 — Emotional Experience Principles' in h2 weight 700, left-aligned.
Blue accent line below.

4 emotional design principle cards in grid-2 layout:

Card 1 (blue border, icon 'sentiment_satisfied'): Title 'Emotional Copywriting' · Body: 'Every word in the interface carries emotional weight. Error messages acknowledge frustration before offering solutions. Success states celebrate outcomes, not features. Empty states inspire possibility, not abandonment. Copy speaks to the human, not the feature.'

Card 2 (purple border, icon 'favorite'): Title 'Loss Aversion Design' · Body: 'Leverage the psychological principle that people feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains. Frame intelligence as risk prevention: '3 accounts showing early churn signals' is more motivating than '47 accounts stable.' Use urgency with precision — not manipulation.'

Card 3 (green border, icon 'workspace_premium'): Title 'Endowment Effect' · Body: 'Users who feel ownership of their intelligence workspace engage more deeply. Personal intelligence preferences, saved views, and customized briefings create investment. The system adapts to the user — the user does not adapt to the system.'

Card 4 (amber border, icon 'support_agent'): Title 'Compassionate Error Handling' · Body: 'When the system cannot deliver intelligence, it explains why — not with technical errors, but with human context: 'We could not analyze this account because the data source has not updated in 14 days.' Always offer a path forward. Never leave the user in a dead end.'

Bottom callout (glass-card accent):
'Enterprise Milestone Recognition: When users achieve significant outcomes — first intelligence-driven deal, streak of early signal detection — the system acknowledges it. Not with confetti or sparkle, but with dignified milestone recognition. Premium. Measured. Meaningful.'

Speaker notes: These four emotional design patterns are selected from the 72-point behavioral psychology checklist. They are the first to be implemented because they have the highest impact on trust and engagement. Loss aversion motivates action. Emotional copywriting reduces friction. The endowment effect increases retention. Compassionate error handling prevents abandonment. Together, they make the experience feel human.

├── Color Semantic Map (confidence, priority, domain)
├── Motion Presets (fast, default, smooth, gentle)

Speaker notes: The visual language follows three principles: premium dark enterprise aesthetic, confidence-coded color system, and atomic component architecture. Every visual element serves the intelligence briefing paradigm. The component system follows atomic design — tokens, atoms, molecules, organisms — ensuring consistency and composability across all 7 experiences.

What should I do? Why trust this? The Intelligence Hub transforms this from a data display into an executive briefing. The same intelligence exists — but it is now structured, prioritized, and actionable. We are not removing intelligence. We are making intelligence usable.
